title: KHILADI — What the evidence supports
source: User-supplied accepted methodology; analytical pipeline not rerun in this animation workspace.
website: Deferred by user; no invented website footage.

scenes.caption: My first IPL team.
scenes.narration: You're in school. You're supposed to be doing maths. But you've got something way more important to figure out. Your IPL best eleven. And honestly? The maths can wait.

scenes.caption: Then came the hackathon.
scenes.narration: Years pass. The cricket notebook survives. Then you see the Rajasthan Royals SupeRR Selector challenge. Your imaginary selections suddenly need something rather inconvenient. Evidence.

scenes.caption: 200,999 events. First: clean.
scenes.narration: Your first obstacle: two hundred thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine delivery events. Wides. No-balls. Run-outs. Rain. Before you judge a player, you have to reconstruct the match correctly.

scenes.caption: Judge the situation BEFORE the ball.
scenes.narration: So you freeze time before every ball. Score. Wickets. Balls remaining. No peeking at the six that happens next. That would be cheating, with a spreadsheet.

scenes.caption: Difficult ≠ consequential.
scenes.narration: But difficult doesn't always mean consequential. Thirty-nine runs an over? Terrifying. Also, probably over. Two needed off one? Now the next ball can change everything.

scenes.caption: Difficulty + win-probability leverage.
scenes.narration: You combine scoreboard difficulty with win-probability leverage, using context-relative percentiles. Your primary pressure definition selects the top twenty percent within each innings. Not within every phase.

scenes.caption: Performance against expectation.
scenes.narration: Next question: better than what? You estimate expected runs and dismissal risk. Batters earn credit for extra runs and survival. Bowlers, for runs prevented and credited wickets.

scenes.caption: Context. Era. Opposition.
scenes.narration: You adjust for scoring eras and opposition. Then combine runs and wickets with a declared assumption: fifteen runs per wicket. You check ten and twenty too. An assumption deserves a test, not a disguise.

scenes.caption: Small sample? Shrink the claim.
scenes.narration: Then the small samples arrive, wearing enormous confidence. Twenty-five pressure events are not four hundred. Empirical Bayes pulls weakly supported estimates toward the average.

scenes.caption: Pressure quality ≠ pressure delta.
scenes.narration: Performing well under pressure isn't the same as improving because of pressure. You find no validated repeatable bowling pressure delta. The batting delta gains are tiny. A psychological clutch trait remains unproven.

scenes.caption: The holdout challenged the story.
scenes.narration: The unseen twenty-twenty-six season challenges your story. Batting quality shows no positive predictive relationship. Bowling looks promising, but an advantage over ordinary economy isn't established.

scenes.caption: 750 match bootstraps.
scenes.narration: So you resample whole matches, seven hundred and fifty times. Confidence intervals. Rank distributions. A top-ten bootstrap rate measures conditional historical stability. It isn't a prophecy.

scenes.caption: Change assumptions. Watch ranks move.
scenes.narration: Change the pressure definition, and your shortlist changes. Remove a player's best season, and nine names leave each top ten. Those aren't details you get to hide.

scenes.caption: A shortlist, with evidence attached.
scenes.narration: Your primary lists put Jos Buttler and Jasprit Bumrah first. But every name needs exposure, uncertainty and format mix. T-twenty international evidence isn't automatically IPL evidence.

scenes.caption: 20 / 20 rankings reproduced.
scenes.narration: Finally, your report's replay reproduces all twenty rankings and passes forty-one checks. The code repeats. The statistical limitations stay.

scenes.caption: Better questions. Honest answers.
scenes.narration: Your notebook used to ask, who would you pick? Khiladi asks a better question. What does the evidence support... and how sure should you be?
